name: Mental Accounting
description: People categorize and treat money differently depending on its source or intended use, rather than treating it as fully fungible.
design_relevance_note: Explains why users respond differently to identically-valued discounts, credits, and windfalls depending on how they're framed and which 'account' they're mentally assigned to.
prevalence_note: One of behavioral economics' most widely taught concepts, foundational to Thaler's Nobel-cited body of work and standard in UX/pricing design discourse.

findings.description: Consumers evaluate a purchase using both 'acquisition utility' (the standard value of the good relative to its price) and a separate 'transaction utility' (the perceived value of the deal itself, relative to a reference price) — coded as gains/losses via the prospect-theory value function — so identical goods can be judged differently depending on perceived deal fairness, and money is mentally partitioned into non-fungible 'accounts' (e.g. housing, food, windfall) governed by an implicit household budgeting process rather than treated as a single fungible pool.

Mental accounting comprises three components — (1) how outcomes are perceived, coded, and evaluated ex ante/ex post; (2) the assignment of income and expenditures to specific labeled accounts and budgets (e.g. housing, food); and (3) the frequency and scope with which accounts are balanced ('choice bracketing', e.g. daily vs. yearly, narrow vs. broad) — and each component causes people to violate the economic principle that money is fungible, which in turn measurably influences real spending, saving, and consumption choices.

applications.title: Duke Credit Union's 'Rainy Day Savings' mental-account experiment -- an honest null result
applications.description: Dan Ariely's Center for Advanced Hindsight partnered with Duke Credit Union (~16,000 members) to test whether creating a specifically labeled 'Rainy Day Savings' mental account, auto-opened by default for half of new members (vs. opt-in for the rest), would increase emergency savings. Over 1,500 new accounts were randomized between January-October 2017; 750 received the labeled sub-account by default, and half of those kept it open. The result: the researchers found no significant difference in savings behavior (balance, deposit frequency/amount, withdrawal frequency/amount) between the opt-in and opt-out conditions, though the treatment-on-the-treated subgroup (opt-out members who kept the account) showed a slight increase they could not confidently attribute to the mental-accounting mechanism itself versus selection bias.
applications.ethical_note: A transparent, consent-respecting field experiment (members could close the account at any time, no fees or penalties) aimed at helping low-income households build emergency savings -- and the researchers disclosed the null result rather than suppressing it, a useful honesty-calibration example for this project's own dialectic-verification mission.

applications.title: The 'Hamburger Paradox': how partitioned pricing changes the 'pain of paying' at an identical total price
applications.description: A teaching illustration contrasting two ways of reaching the same price -- a single bundled price (a whole burger for 15 EUR) versus a base price plus itemized add-ons (a build-your-own burger, or an airline ticket, or a B2B software plan, each summing to the same total through priced extras) -- showing that itemized pricing, even at an identical total, increases the perceived 'pain of paying' and the cognitive effort of the purchase decision, though it can also enable genuine personalization when designed well.
applications.industry_context: e-commerce / pricing psychology (illustrated across restaurant, travel, and B2B SaaS examples)
applications.ethical_note: Every price shown in each illustrative scenario is genuine and disclosed -- this isn't a deception case. But the entire premise is that identical prices can be made to feel more or less painful through structuring alone, which is a deliberate lever over perception, not neutral information design. Included as a teaching example specifically because it names the tradeoff honestly (partitioning can enable genuine personalization or feel like nickel-and-diming, depending on execution) rather than presenting only the persuasive upside.
